title: Dynamical quantum simulations as laboratories for quantum information
authors: Su Yeon Chang, Hailey S. Murray, Brian Barch, Greeshma Oruganti, Luis Pedro García-Pintos, Martin Larocca, Mark M. Wilde, M. Cerezo
abstract: Dynamical quantum simulations are commonly designed to access a particular response function or correlation function. Yet the underlying protocol prepares a family of many-body states that contains information well beyond the observable for which the simulation was originally designed. In this work, we explore the idea of using these states as laboratories for quantum information. As a case study, we consider the local-pulse protocols used to compute Green functions in finite XX and XXX spin chains, and we interpret opposite source rotations as encoding a classical bit into the many-body system. This allows us to follow how the resulting record propagates, how it is encoded across local subsystems, and how readily it can be accessed with different measurements. We also find a clear separation between representation and readout. While fermionic covariance data exactly reconstruct the signed response in the XX chain, simple spin measurements recover a larger fraction of the locally available information in the XXX chain. This reversed ordering persists when we move from finite-pulse discrimination to local source-angle estimation. Going beyond the source record, the same reduced states also allow us to reinterpret results in terms of Bell state recovery and quantum communication rates, as well as providing direct access to the evolving bipartite and genuine multipartite entanglement of the system. Our results show that dynamical quantum simulations developed for response calculations can naturally be used to ask a much broader set of quantum-information questions about the many-body states they already prepare.
summary: This work proposes viewing dynamical quantum simulations not just as tools to measure specific correlation functions, but as sources of rich quantum information. By analyzing the states prepared during these simulations on spin chains, the authors demonstrate how to extract entanglement measures and communication capacities. This shifts the focus from the measurement target to the inherent quantum resources within the system.
main_problem: To reframe dynamical quantum simulations, typically designed for specific response functions, as general 'laboratories' for exploring quantum information properties encoded in the prepared many-body states.
main_result: The prepared states allow for the direct calculation of quantum information measures like entanglement and communication rates, revealing a separation between state representation and physical readout.
method: The authors analyze local-pulse protocols on spin chains, interpreting source rotations as encoding classical bits and quantifying information flow using measures like trace distance and Holevo information.
model_or_system: The study uses local-pulse protocols to compute Green functions in finite XX and XXX spin chains, analyzing the resulting many-body states prepared by the dynamics.
key_observables: Bipartite and genuine multipartite entanglement, Bell state recovery rates, quantum communication rates, Holevo information ($\chi_R$), and trace distance ($\Delta_R$).
important_parameters: The spin chain type (XX vs. XXX), the size of the local observation region ($R$), and the pulse parameters defining the source rotation.
main_assumptions: The framework assumes that the dynamics prepare a rich family of many-body states that can be interrogated beyond the initially targeted observable.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically contrasts the conventional view (measuring a target observable) with the proposed view (using prepared states for information analysis).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the conceptual shift (from observable to state) to applying this framework to specific spin chain models (XX/XXX), and finally extending the analysis to general quantum information measures like entanglement and capacity.
why_interesting: It provides a powerful, general methodology for extracting deep quantum information—like entanglement structure—from standard, routine measurements in condensed matter simulations, connecting dynamics directly to quantum information theory.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Schematic representation of our framework. A dynamical quantum simulation prepares a family of rich many-body states as the system evolves. In the conventional view, these states are used to estimate a target dynamical quantity, such as a response function or spectrum that can be compared with experiment. Here we instead take the pre- pared states themselves as objects of study and use them to investigate quantum-information properties such as informa- tion propagation, encoding and readout, and entanglement structure.

Figure 2. Trace distance wakes for all observation apertures. Trace distance maps for XX (a-d) and XXX (e-h) at widths k = 1, 3, 5, 7. Every panel uses the same absolute scale. At fixed time and center, the regions are nested, so enlarging the aperture cannot reduce the distinguishability. The maps locate the record over the space-time window.

Figure 3. Trace distance at the source as a function of time for the four observation apertures k = 1, 3, 5, 7. Solid (dashed) lines correspond to the XX (XXX) chain, with colors indicating the aperture size. For k = 1, the trace distance is directly related to the conventional local retarded response through ∆1(t) = 2|GR zz(j0, j0; t)|. Increasing the aperture reveals a substantially larger and longer-lived record of the same perturbation. The more persistent oscillatory structure in XXX follows that of the quantum-wake behavior of the isotropic Heisenberg chain.

Figure 4. Holevo-information wakes for all observation apertures. The layout and absolute spatial and temporal scales are the same as in Fig. 2. The same propagating structure is visible, but regions of small distinguishability are strongly suppressed because χR is quadratic in ∆R when the two local branches are close. For k = 1, where ∆1 is proportional to the magnitude of the local retarded Green function, this implies χ1 ∝|GR zz|2 in this regime.

Figure 5. Weak-signal scaling and aperture dependence of the trace distance and Holevo information. Panels (a) and (b) show XR as a function of ∆2 R for the XX and XXX chains, respectively, restricted to 10−5 ≤∆R ≤0.05. Colors denote the aperture width k, and solid lines show independent power-law fits XR ∝(∆2 R)m. The fitted exponents remain close to m = 1 for every model and aperture, confirming the quadratic scaling XR ∝∆2 R when the two local branches are nearly indistinguishable. Panels (c) and (d) show the median ∆R and XR, respectively, as a function of k, with shaded regions indicating the 5th–95th percentile range over the resolved space-time points.
